An LLM's **context window** is the maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, that the model can take in at once. That includes the system prompt, the conversation history, tool definitions, tool results, retrieved documents and the model's own output. The model can't see anything outside this window and has no other working memory, so whatever isn't in the context doesn't exist for that call. This matters a lot for agents because they run long loops. Each step adds tool calls, file contents, search results and reasoning, so the context fills up fast. Once it's full, you have to drop, summarize or compress earlier material, and you risk losing important instructions or facts. Even before the limit, very long contexts raise cost and latency and can lower quality, because relevant details get buried in noise. Good agent design treats context as a scarce budget. Common techniques are:
- retrieving only what's relevant
- summarizing or trimming old turns
- keeping tool outputs short
- handing subtasks to subagents with fresh contexts
- storing durable state in external memory or files instead of the prompt
